Distributions

Source: vignettes/articles/distributions.Rmd
distributions.Rmd

Charts that show how a numeric variable is spread: where values concentrate, how wide the spread is, and how several groups differ.

Chart Use it when
histogram() You look at the distribution of a single numeric variable
violin_plot() You compare distributions across groups, with quartiles
beeswarm_plot() You want to show every observation, not only a summary
ridgeline_plot() You compare the distributions of many groups
animated_histogram() You present a distribution and want the bars to grow on click

histogram()

histogram() shows how a numeric variable is spread, as bars counting the observations in bins of equal width. Give it a vector, or a data frame and the name of a column. The bins get round widths, and a summary of the data (number of observations, mean, median, standard deviation) is shown above the bars.

histogram(
  x      = mpg$hwy,
  title  = "Highway fuel economy",
  xtitle = "Miles per gallon"
)

The chart is interactive:

  • the − / + buttons change the number of bins, and Count / % switches between counts and percentages;
  • hovering a bin shows its range, its count, its share of the total and the share of the observations up to that bin;
  • dragging across the bars selects a range, and the summary then describes the selected observations. Zoom re-bins the data inside the range (useful for long tails); double-click to go back.

Add a density curve with density = TRUE (or "normal" for a fitted normal curve), mean and median lines with stats, and thresholds with refLines. binWidth sets the width of the bins, and xPrefix, xSuffix and xFormat format the values:

histogram(
  x        = "price",
  data     = diamonds,
  bins     = 50,
  density  = TRUE,
  stats    = c("mean", "median"),
  xPrefix  = "$",
  xFormat  = ",.0f",
  title    = "Diamond prices",
  subtitle = "Drag across the bars to select a range, then zoom in"
)

With group, the bars are split by group, stacked or overlaid (switch with the buttons). stat = "percent" with overlaid groups divides each group by its own size, so groups of different sizes can be compared. Click a legend entry to hide a group, double-click it to isolate it:

histogram(
  x        = "hwy",
  data     = mpg,
  group    = "drv",
  position = "overlay",
  stat     = "percent",
  binWidth = 2,
  density  = TRUE,
  fill     = c("4" = "#4269d0", f = "#efb118", r = "#ff725c"),
  title    = "Highway fuel economy by drive train"
)

breaks gives bins of unequal widths (the bars then show densities, so their areas stay comparable), and rug = TRUE draws a tick for every observation:

histogram(
  x       = faithful$eruptions,
  breaks  = c(1.5, 2, 2.5, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5.5),
  rug     = TRUE,
  title   = "Old Faithful eruptions",
  xtitle  = "Duration (minutes)",
  xSuffix = " min"
)

In Shiny, input$<id>_clicked returns the clicked bin and input$<id>_selected the selected range.

violin_plot()

violin_plot() reproduces the look of Plotly.js violin traces. Each group gets a mirrored kernel density, with an optional inner box plot, jittered raw points, and a hover tooltip showing the summary statistics.

violin_plot(
  data   = iris,
  y      = "Sepal.Length",
  group  = "Species",
  title  = "Sepal length by species",
  ytitle = "Sepal length (cm)"
)

Use points = "all" to show every observation, meanline to mark the mean, sort to order the violins, and scale = "count" to make each violin’s width proportional to its group size:

violin_plot(
  data         = mpg,
  y            = "hwy",
  group        = "class",
  points       = "all",
  meanline     = TRUE,
  sort         = "median",
  colorPalette = "Tableau10",
  title        = "Highway fuel economy by vehicle class",
  ytitle       = "Highway miles per gallon"
)

beeswarm_plot()

A beeswarm plot shows every individual data point along a numeric axis, spreading them sideways so they never overlap. It is far more transparent than a box plot because nothing is hidden behind a summary statistic — you see the full shape, outliers, and clusters of the raw data. The New York Times graphics desk uses this style regularly to remind readers that numbers represent real people.

The layout is computed with a D3 force simulation: each point is pulled toward its true value on the x-axis while a collision force prevents any two circles from touching.

library(ggplot2) # for the mpg dataset

# Single swarm — full distribution of highway fuel economy
beeswarm_plot(
  data   = mpg,
  x      = "hwy",
  col    = "steelblue",
  xtitle = "Highway miles per gallon",
  title  = "Distribution of hwy"
)

When a group column is provided, one swarm is drawn per group and colored automatically:

beeswarm_plot(
  data   = mpg,
  x      = "hwy",
  group  = "class",
  xtitle = "Highway miles per gallon",
  title  = "Highway fuel economy by vehicle class", 
  tooltip = "manufacturer"
)

You can swap the dataset and adjust the look freely. Here using the built-in iris dataset with a different color palette and larger points:

beeswarm_plot(
  data         = iris,
  x            = "Sepal.Length",
  group        = "Species",
  colorPalette = "Set2",
  radius       = 5,
  opacity      = 0.8,
  xtitle       = "Sepal length (cm)",
  title        = "Sepal length by species"
)

ridgeline_plot()

A ridgeline plot, also known as a “joy plot”, stacks several partially overlapping density curves, one per group, on a shared x-axis. The nickname comes from the cover of Joy Division’s 1979 album Unknown Pleasures, which reproduces a 1970 plot of successive radio pulses from the first discovered pulsar. Claus Wilke’s ggridges package made the format popular, and FiveThirtyEight and The Washington Post use it often. It is a good way to compare the shape of many distributions at once (shifts, spread, bimodality) without the space a grid of histograms would need.

The densities are computed in the browser with a Gaussian (default) or Epanechnikov kernel. By default, one joint bandwidth is picked from the pooled data with Silverman’s rule of thumb, so every ridge is smoothed the same way. Lower ridges are drawn in front of the ones above them. Hovering a ridge or its label brings it to the front and shows its number of observations and mean.

set.seed(2026)

reaction <- data.frame(
  time = c(rnorm(200, 300, 40), rnorm(200, 340, 50),
           rnorm(200, 380, 35), c(rnorm(100, 360, 25), rnorm(100, 460, 30)),
           rnorm(200, 420, 60)),
  condition = rep(c("Baseline", "Noise", "Fatigue", "Dual task", "Night"),
                  each = 200)
)

ridgeline_plot(
  data   = reaction,
  x      = "time",
  group  = "condition",
  sort   = "mean",
  stat   = "median",
  title  = "Reaction time by condition",
  xtitle = "Reaction time (ms)"
)

Use overlap to control how far each ridge reaches into the one above it, and fill, fillOpacity and lineCol to change the look. fill can be a single colour or a named vector with one colour per group:

library(ggplot2) # for the mpg dataset

ridgeline_plot(
  data        = mpg,
  x           = "hwy",
  group       = "class",
  sort        = "median",
  fill        = "#2c7fb8",
  lineCol     = "white",
  fillOpacity = 0.9,
  overlap     = 2,
  title       = "Highway fuel economy by vehicle class",
  xtitle      = "Highway miles per gallon"
)

animated_histogram()

This function allows you to create a one-click histogram animation. Useful for presentation purposes. Click on the following empty plot and see what happens:

animated_histogram(
  x = mpg$hwy,
  duration = 2000,
  delay = 100,
  fill = "lime",
  stroke = "white",
  bgcol = "white"
  )

Note that you can customize the animation using the two parameters duration and delay.
